title: Search Suggestions System
description: Brute force to optimized: filtering and sorting fresh per prefix versus sorting once and binary searching per prefix.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given an array of product names and a search word, return a list of lists: for each prefix of searchWord (as if a user typed it character by character), the up to three lexicographically smallest products from products that start with that prefix.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","products array, searchWord"],["Output","For each prefix of searchWord (length 1 up to full length), up to 3 lexicographically smallest matching product names"],["Goal","Sort products once, then efficiently find matches for each growing prefix"],["Constraints","Up to 1000 products, searchWord up to 1000 characters"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Suggestions after each character typed, lexicographically smallest first\"","Sort products once so lexicographic order matches array order, then binary search for each prefix"],["\"Up to 3 matches, prefix growing one character at a time\"","Since products are sorted, once the binary search finds the first matching index, the next up to 2 entries (if they still match the prefix) are the answer"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Sorting products alphabetically ONCE means that for any prefix, all products starting with that prefix appear as a contiguous block in the sorted array. Binary searching for where that prefix would be inserted immediately locates the start of that block, and the first up to three entries within it (checked to actually match the prefix) are the answer.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Sorted Phone Book and a Growing Search Term
blocks.text: Picture a phone book sorted alphabetically. As a search term grows one letter at a time, flipping to where that term would be inserted (via a bisecting search) immediately reveals the next few entries that could still match, without rescanning the entire book from the start each time.

blocks.caption: Sort products once, then binary search the sorted list for each growing prefix

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: products = ["mobile", "mouse", "moneypot", "monitor", "mousepad"], searchWord = "mouse"

Result: [["mobile","moneypot","monitor"],["mobile","moneypot","monitor"],["mouse","mousepad"],["mouse","mousepad"],["mouse","mousepad"]]. Sorted products are moneypot, mobile, monitor, mouse, mousepad; after typing "m", the three smallest are mobile, moneypot, monitor; after "mo" the same three still apply; after "mou", "mous", "mouse" only mouse and mousepad match.
5. How Should We Think?

Before filtering the FULL products list by startsWith separately for every single prefix typed, notice that sorting products once turns every prefix's matches into one CONTIGUOUS block in the sorted array, locatable via binary search.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Sorting products alphabetically means all products sharing any given prefix sit in one contiguous run in the sorted array.

Observation 2: Binary searching for the position where the current prefix would be inserted (lower bound) lands exactly at the start of that contiguous run, if any products match.

Observation 3: From that starting position, checking up to the next 3 entries (stopping early if one no longer starts with the prefix) gives the required up to 3 lexicographically smallest matches.

Observation 4: Repeating this per character of searchWord (building the prefix incrementally) reuses the SAME sorted array throughout, needing no re-filtering of the whole list each time.
This leads to sorting products once, then for each prefix of searchWord, binary searching for its lower bound and collecting up to 3 valid matches from there.
6. Brute Force Solution
For each prefix of searchWord, filter the entire products array directly for names starting with that prefix, sort the matches, and take the first three.

codes.python:
def suggested_products_brute(products, search_word):
    result = []
    prefix = ''
    for c in search_word:
        prefix += c
        matches = sorted(p for p in products if p.startswith(prefix))    # filter ALL products every time
        result.append(matches[:3])
    return result

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Filtering and sorting matches fresh for every prefix implements the definition simply.
This repeats a full O(n) scan (plus sorting) for every character typed, wasteful since sorting products just once upfront already groups all prefix matches together.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(searchWord length times (n times average product length plus n log n sorting)).
Space: O(n) per filtered/sorted list.
Limitation: sorting products once upfront and binary searching per prefix avoids repeated full scans and repeated sorting.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Sort products alphabetically ONCE. For each growing prefix of searchWord, binary search the sorted array for the lower bound of the prefix (the first index where a product would be greater than or equal to the prefix). Starting from that index, check up to the next 3 products, keeping those that still start with the prefix, and stop early once one does not.
Sort products once; for each prefix, binary search for its lower bound and collect up to 3 valid matches starting there.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run (sorted products: mobile, moneypot, monitor, mouse, mousepad)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Prefix","Lower bound index","Up to 3 matches"],"rows":[["m","0","mobile, moneypot, monitor"],["mo","0","mobile, moneypot, monitor"],["mou","3","mouse, mousepad"],["mous","3","mouse, mousepad"],["mouse","3","mouse, mousepad"]]}

blocks.text: Why This Works

Because products are sorted, every product sharing a given prefix occupies one contiguous run starting at the prefix's lower-bound position. Binary search locates that starting position in logarithmic time, and checking only the next up to three entries (stopping the moment one no longer matches) correctly and efficiently gathers the required lexicographically smallest matches, all without ever re-filtering or re-sorting the full product list again.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n) to sort once, O(searchWord length times log n) for all the binary searches.
Space: O(n) for the sorted copy, O(searchWord length) for the output.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Search Suggestions System is a classic "sort once, binary search per query" technique, closely related to trie-based prefix matching but solvable without an explicit trie.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to sort products before binary searching, which breaks the contiguous-block property entirely.
Not stopping early when an entry within the next 3 no longer actually starts with the current prefix.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["No product matches a given prefix","That prefix's list in the output is empty."],["Fewer than 3 products match a prefix","All matching products are returned, without padding."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "sorting groups every prefix's matches into one contiguous block, found via binary search" demonstrates the key structural insight clearly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "suggest matches after each character typed, lexicographically smallest first", think: sort once, then binary search for each growing prefix's lower bound.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you solve this with an explicit trie instead, storing the top 3 suggestions at each trie node during construction?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Implement Trie and other prefix-based lookup problems; also a classic binary search application (lower bound).

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The filter-and-sort-per-prefix approach costs O(searchWord length times n log n); the sort-once-then-binary-search approach costs O(n log n plus searchWord length times log n), the standard efficient solution.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: sort once, binary search per query (lower bound).
Core Idea: sorted products group every prefix's matches into one contiguous run, found via binary search.
Time: O(searchWord length times n log n) for the brute force, O(n log n plus searchWord length times log n) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: sorting once transforms repeated full scans into fast binary searches.
Interview Difficulty: a practical binary search/prefix-matching problem.
One line memory trick: sort once, then bisect for each prefix.
